description: We are an interdisciplinary team passionate about space, technology, and solving challenging real-world problems. We’re looking for motivated teammates with skills in aerospace, physics, electronics, mathematics, AI/ML, or other relevant fields. We value creativity, collaboration, initiative, and a commitment to turning ambitious ideas into reality.
summary:
AEGIS is an autonomous crew health officer for deep-space missions, built by Team Orbynex. On the way to Mars, a message to Earth can take up to 22 minutes each way, so astronauts cannot wait for a doctor’s real-time advice. AEGIS helps the crew spot, understand and act on health problems themselves.

It is a browser app that works fully offline. Astronauts log quick check-ins, simple tests, guided self-exams and eye scans across 8 body systems and 21 health indicators. AEGIS rates each reading green, amber or red using thresholds that change with the mission: ISS, Moon, Mars transit or Mars surface. A rules engine spots risks that only appear in combination, such as headaches together with high cabin CO₂. It also catches slow drift away from each astronaut’s own baseline. Every finding comes with NASA-based countermeasures in plain words. Follow-ups show whether things improved, and a clear report is queued for flight surgeons across the communication delay. Live NASA space weather data adds radiation awareness.

As crews travel farther from Earth, health autonomy becomes essential. AEGIS turns raw readings into confident decisions on board.
details:
What it does and how it works

AEGIS is an autonomous crew health officer: a health-monitoring app built for long missions where Earth is too far away to give real-time medical help. Astronauts record their health in four ways:

  • quick daily check-ins on sleep, mood, symptoms and workload
  • simple tests
  • guided self-exams
  • webcam-assisted eye scans

These cover 8 body systems and 21 health indicators.

Each reading is checked against thresholds that change with the mission: ISS, Moon, Mars transit or Mars surface. It is then rated green, amber or red.

A rules engine looks for risks that only show up together, such as headaches combined with high cabin CO₂. It also watches each astronaut’s personal baseline to catch slow drift that one-off checks miss.

Every finding comes with:

  • a plain-language explanation
  • NASA-based countermeasures
  • a follow-up that shows whether things are improving, staying the same or getting worse

AEGIS also writes a structured report for flight surgeons in a standard medical handover format (SBAR: Situation, Background, Assessment, Recommendation). The report is queued across the communication delay. Live NASA space weather data (DONKI) adds radiation awareness, with a stored snapshot for when there is no connection.

Benefits

  • Works fully offline, which matters when Earth is minutes away.
  • Explains why something matters and what to do now, not just raw numbers.
  • Readings stay on the device.
  • Personal baselines mean each astronaut is judged against their own normal.
  • Runs on any laptop or tablet, with nothing to install.

Intended impact
Missions to the Moon and Mars will need crews to manage their own health. AEGIS helps three groups:

  • Astronauts without medical training can act with confidence.
  • Crew medical officers get one view of the whole crew, with early warnings.
  • Flight surgeons receive clear before-and-after reports despite the delay.

The same approach could help remote expeditions, polar stations and isolated communities on Earth.

Tools and technologies

  • HTML, CSS and JavaScript, as a single file with no build step
  • Browser storage (localStorage), plus a service worker and manifest so it installs as an offline app
  • NASA DONKI API for space weather
  • The browser webcam API for guided scans
  • Playwright with headless Chrome for testing
  • GitHub for version control; deployed at orbynex-aegis.health

No special hardware is needed. A laptop or tablet with a webcam is enough.

Creativity
Instead of a dashboard of charts, AEGIS acts like an on-board medical officer. It finds the most important issue, says what to do now, and checks later whether it worked. The mission-aware thresholds, the combined-risk rules and a report designed around the Earth delay are built specifically for deep-space operations.

Factors our team considered

  • Communication delay: up to 22 minutes each way to Mars.
  • NASA research: the Human Research Program’s five hazards of spaceflight, plus NASA’s CO₂ and radiation limits.
  • Crew without medical training: the app is usable by astronauts who aren’t doctors.
  • Mission differences: gravity, delay, radiation and exercise needs change with each environment.
  • Privacy: readings stay on the device.
  • Honesty: AEGIS is a prototype, not a medical device. Demo data is simulated and clearly labelled, and real limits would be set by flight surgeons.
